title: The Semi-Recent History of Exercise
summary: Hosts trace the modern history of exercise, arguing it is a relatively recent mainstream phenomenon. They cover mid-century attitudes toward exercise and its risks, Jeremy Morris's bus-driver/conductor study, the corporate health boom, and the rise of jogging (Arthur Lydiard, Bill Bowerman, Jim Fixx, President Jimmy Carter's running). They then discuss aerobics (Kenneth Cooper, Jackie Sorenson, Gilda Marx's Body by Gilda, Jane Fonda, Judy Shepherd's Jazzercise, Richard Simmons), health clubs (Jack LaLanne, Vic Tanny, Nautilus, Gold's Gym, Bally Total Fitness, 24 Hour Fitness, Curves), and later trends like yoga, Pilates, barre, boot camp, Tae Bo, Tabata/HIIT, Zumba and CrossFit. A listener mail correction about the Colosseum's hypogeum closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening and premise
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the history of exercise and note that organized exercise is a fairly recent development in America, though people exercised in earlier times.

segments.title: Early attitudes toward exercise and the Morris bus study
segments.summary: Mid-twentieth-century Americans rarely exercised and were often seen as weird or gay; women were discouraged from exercise. Exercise was thought to be dangerous, but British epidemiologist Jeremy Morris compared bus drivers and conductors and found drivers had about twice as many heart attacks, helping start the idea that exercise is good for the heart.

segments.title: Exercise boom origins and corporate health concerns
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1960s-1980s rise in exercise, the role of sedentary desk jobs, and a mid-1970s Fortune article about heart attacks among executives costing firms money. They note education gaps in exercise rates today.

segments.title: Fitness and empowerment in the 1980s
segments.summary: Fitness became geared toward women through feminism, Title IX, and changing beauty standards for men and women.

segments.title: Jogging origins and Arthur Lydiard
segments.summary: Jogging grew out of competitive running. New Zealand coach Arthur Lydiard developed marathon training methods in the 1960s that laid groundwork for jogging, and early joggers were quite hardcore.

segments.title: Bill Bowerman, Jogging book, and jogging in the 1970s
segments.summary: Bill Bowerman, Oregon running coach and Nike co-founder, published a pamphlet and then the book Jogging with cardiologist W. E. Harris. A 1968 New York Times article covered joggers' encounters with police and night running. Jim Fixx's 1977 Complete Book of Running popularized jogging; Fixx died while jogging. Jimmy Carter jogged as president, nearly collapsing during a Camp David fun run. A late-1990s New York Times retrospective noted running was still a subculture into the 1970s.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the aerobics segment.

segments.title: Kenneth Cooper and the origins of aerobics
segments.summary: Air Force surgeon Kenneth Cooper introduced aerobic exercise in the 1960s and wrote the 1968 book Aerobics. Jackie Sorenson, a dance teacher and Air Force wife in Puerto Rico, created a dance-based aerobics class in 1969 that became a TV show called Aerobic Dancing.

segments.title: Jazzercise and the boutique fitness franchise model
segments.summary: Judy Shepherd founded Jazzercise, which became a franchise and was the second-biggest franchise company in the US in 1984. Her model of branded exercise studios in strip malls is seen as the start of boutique fitness franchising.

segments.title: Gilda Marx, Body by Gilda, and Jane Fonda's workout
segments.summary: Gilda Marx created an exercise routine for dancers that grew into Body by Gilda, with clients including Jane Fonda and Richard Simmons. Jane Fonda's Workout Book was a bestseller and her workout VHS tape was the top non-movie VHS seller, with about 17 million copies sold across the set.

segments.title: Richard Simmons and Sweating to the Oldies
segments.summary: Richard Simmons, who began at Body by Gilda, founded his own business, had his own TV show, and released Sweating to the Oldies, described as the best-selling home fitness video. The hosts also mention his Congressional testimony and Letterman appearances.

segments.title: Deal-A-Meal and Richard Simmons' persona
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Richard Simmons' Deal-A-Meal weight-loss program and his personality, along with a note about his later life.

segments.title: Personal anecdotes about aerobics and home exercise
segments.summary: Host Chuck recalls his mother's aerobics involvement during an unhappy marriage in the 1980s, and Josh recalls home exercise gadgets such as the Thigh Master and mini trampolines.

segments.title: Gym history, Jack LaLanne, and Vic Tanny health clubs
segments.summary: The word gymnasium comes from the Greek for naked. Jack LaLanne opened a health club in Oakland in 1939, and Vic Tanny opened a gym in Santa Monica the same year. Tanny's health clubs became huge in the 1970s and 1980s, with pools, racquetball courts and other amenities, and his chain later went out of business.

segments.title: Nautilus machines and early gym chains
segments.summary: Nautilus bought up closed Vic Tanny locations and marketed its machines as weight training that was less intimidating than free weights. Arthur Jones created Nautilus machines promoting workouts to temporary muscle failure in less time.

segments.title: Gold's Gym, Bally Total Fitness, and monthly memberships
segments.summary: Gold's Gym, founded by bodybuilder Joe Gold, became known for serious lifting. Bally Total Fitness, founded by former Vic Tanny employee Donna Hugh Wildman, was known for predatory contracts. 24 Hour Fitness, under Mark Mastrov, introduced monthly memberships.

segments.title: Curves and women-only fitness clubs
segments.summary: Women-only fitness clubs existed by the 1960s, but Curves, started by Gary and Diane Heavenrich, targeted women over forty-five and became a large fitness franchise. LA Fitness is noted as a leader in revenue.

segments.title: Yoga and Pilates
segments.summary: Yoga was introduced to the US in the 19th century and boomed through PBS shows, with at least 100,000 studios in the US, mostly independently owned. Pilates was named after Joseph Pilates, a German circus performer interned in the UK during World War One, who developed stretching-based exercises.

segments.title: Barre, boot camp, and Tae Bo
segments.summary: Barre was created by German ballerina Lotte Berk, who blended ballet, yoga and Pilates and had a free-love message. Boot camp workouts grew in the 1990s. Tae Bo was created by Billy Blanks, a US karate team captain, and promoted via infomercial.

segments.title: Tabata, Japanese radio calisthenics, and Zumba origins
segments.summary: Tabata, named after sports scientist Izumi Tabata, is a high-intensity interval training format of short bursts with brief rests. Japan's radio taiso daily exercise broadcasts are mentioned. Zumba was started by Alberto Perez in Colombia in the mid-1990s when he played music he had on hand.

segments.title: CrossFit and closing thoughts on exercise
segments.summary: CrossFit is described as an intense workout combining weightlifting and gymnastics, popular with a devoted following. Hosts share personal experiences and conclude exercise is good for mental health even if not for weight loss.

segments.title: Listener mail: Colosseum hypogeum
segments.summary: A listener correction says the hypogeum under the Colosseum was built after the amphitheater, so the arena could no longer be flooded for mock naval battles once it was dug.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off with a reminder to send email to the show and a note that the show is an iHeartRadio production.
